extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners, USPTO Office of Enrollment and Discipline (OED) staff, and attorneys subject to USPTO discipline
extracted.subtask_description: Standards, procedures, and sanctions governing disciplinary action against patent practitioners before the USPTO, including jurisdictional bases, applicable professional-conduct rules, grounds for discipline (including reciprocal state discipline), and remedies such as suspension and publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO jurisdiction for disciplinary matters
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Director has jurisdiction over disciplinary matters pursuant to 35 U.S.C. §§ 2(b)(2)(D) and 32, and 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.19 and 11.26.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disciplinary actions against registered patent practitioners are governed by the cited statutory and regulatory provisions; jurisdictional citations should be included in orders and settlement documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicable professional-conduct rules by date
rubrics_metrics.description: To the extent alleged conduct occurred prior to May 3, 2013, the USPTO Code of Professional Responsibility (37 C.F.R. §§ 10.20-10.112) is applicable; effective May 3, 2013, the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.101-11.901) apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine which version of the Rules applies based on the date of the conduct; cite the appropriate regulatory scheme when alleging rule violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(h) — public discipline by a State as grounds for USPTO discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Being publicly disciplined on ethical grounds by a duly constituted authority of a State constitutes a violation of 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(h).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reciprocal or disciplinary action by state courts/boards can trigger USPTO disciplinary proceedings under § 11.804(h); USPTO may base discipline on the state decision and related stipulated facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: 20:1.3 — reasonable diligence and promptness in representing a client
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 20:1.3 (failure to act with reasonable diligence and promptness in representing a client) was cited as a basis for state suspension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of diligence (e.g., failing to perform work after taking fees) is an ethical violation that can support disciplinary sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 20:1.4(a)(3) and (4) — communication with client
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules 20:1.4(a)(3) and (4) (failure to keep a client reasonably informed about the status of a matter and failure to promptly comply with reasonable requests for information) were cited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to keep clients informed or to respond promptly to client requests is an actionable misconduct ground; examples include not communicating status or ignoring client inquiries.

rubrics_metrics.name: 20:1.5(a) — unreasonable fees
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 20:1.5(a) (unreasonable fees) was cited as a basis for discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Charging or retaining fees that are unreasonable may lead to suspension or other sanctions; fee reasonableness should be documented and defensible.

rubrics_metrics.name: 20:1.5(b)(1) and (2) — communicating scope of representation and fees
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules 20:1.5(b)(1) and (2) (failure to communicate the scope of representation and fees) were cited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must communicate clearly about the scope of representation and fee arrangements; failure to do so is an ethical violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 20:1.15(d)(1) and (2) — proper disbursement of client funds
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules 20:1.15(d)(1) and (2) (failure to properly disburse funds received) were cited as misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must handle and disburse client funds properly (trust account requirements); mishandling client funds is a serious ethical violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 20:1.16(d) — protecting client's interest upon termination
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 20:1.16(d) (failure to protect a client's interest upon termination of representation) was cited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Upon termination, attorneys must take steps to protect client interests, including returning files and unearned fees; failing to do so can lead to discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: 20:8.4(g) — misconduct by violating an attorney's oath
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 20:8.4(g) (misconduct by violating an attorney's oath) was cited as a ground for state discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violations of the attorney oath or similar fundamental misconduct are recognized bases for professional discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: 22.03(2) & (6) / 20:8.4(h) — failure to cooperate in a disciplinary investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules 22.03(2) and 22.03(6), enforced via 20:8.4(h) (failure to cooperate in a disciplinary investigation), were cited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not cooperating with disciplinary authorities (e.g., failing to provide requested information) is actionable and can aggravate sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal discipline — state suspension can lead to USPTO suspension
rubrics_metrics.description: This action was characterized as a reciprocal disciplinary proceeding: the state suspension by the Supreme Court of Wisconsin resulted in the USPTO ordering suspension for the practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners disciplined by state authorities should expect that the USPTO may impose reciprocal sanctions based on state findings; settlement/reciprocal procedures are available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of stipulated facts and joint legal conclusion to resolve discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: The parties submitted a Proposed Settlement Agreement with stipulated facts and a joint legal conclusion which, when approved by the USPTO Director, resolved the disciplinary action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disciplinary matters may be resolved by settlement agreements that incorporate stipulated facts and admissions; such agreements require approval by the USPTO Director and result in Final Orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanction type — suspension from practice before the USPTO
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent shall be suspended from the practice of patent, trademark and other non-patent law before the USPTO for two years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USPTO sanctions include suspension of practice before the Office for specified durations; the scope of suspension can cover patent, trademark, and other non-patent matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of disciplinary orders and notices
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director shall electronically publish the Final Order at OED's electronic Reading Room and publish a notice in the Official Gazette describing the suspension and the underlying state rules violated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final Orders and notices of suspension are publicly posted (OED Reading Room, Official Gazette) as part of discipline; published notices typically summarize the misconduct and regulatory bases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of disciplinary record in future matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing in the Final Order prevents the Office from considering the record of this disciplinary proceeding (including the Final Order) when addressing any further complaint or evidence of similar misconduct or in any future disciplinary proceeding against the respondent as an aggravating factor or to rebut representations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Past disciplinary findings can be used against a practitioner in later complaints or proceedings and may aggravate future sanctions or rebut claims about fitness or representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocation of costs in settlement
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director and Respondent shall each bear their own costs incurred to date in carrying out the terms of the Agreement and the Final Order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Settlement agreements may specify that each party bears its own costs; cost allocation is an explicit term that can be agreed on in settlements resolving disciplinary matters.
